strengths: Proposes DrVoice, a parallel speech-text voice conversation model with dual-resolution speech representations, using a grouping mechanism to reduce LLM input frame rate to 5Hz and a Speech Refined Head (SRH) to generate ungrouped 25Hz speech tokens.
Introduces CoM-Mixing training with seven multimodal interaction patterns and system prompts, enabling flexible output modes such as text-only, parallel speech-text, and chain-of-modality generation.
Provides ablations on continuous speech encoder, SRH, SRH pretraining, grouping factor, and CoM-Mixing, showing consistent benefits on Llama Questions and reduced training GPU hours with grouping.
Reports competitive results on Spoken QA benchmarks, including strong Llama Questions performance and an efficient small model that outperforms same-size baselines.
Implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, and compute setup are largely provided, and the authors commit to releasing code and checkpoints.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the paper combines existing ideas such as parallel speech-text joint modeling, speech token grouping, a refinement head, and chain-of-modality prompting, with limited conceptual leap beyond prior work like Moshi, GLM-4-Voice, Kimi-Audio, and SpeechGPT.

Evaluation is narrow, covering only two spoken question answering benchmarks; there is no evaluation of full-duplex dialogue, instruction following, conversational quality, general audio, or safety, despite claims about voice conversation systems.

The SOTA claim is marginal and not uniformly supported: average S2T gains over Kimi-Audio are small (75.1 vs. 74.7), average S2S gains over VITA-Audio are small (55.5 vs. 54.9), and DrVoice is worse on Web Questions S2T and S2S than some baselines.

Baselines are not re-evaluated under controlled conditions; many numbers are copied from prior papers with different training data, model sizes, frame rates, and evaluation protocols, undermining direct comparisons and the 'similar size' positioning.

Speech quality is not state-of-the-art: UTMOS is lower than GLM-4-Voice, Moshi, and Llama-Omni, and no human MOS or audio samples are provided, so the claim of SOTA speech foundation modeling is not fully supported.

The low-latency and real-time claims are unsupported: the SRH requires k autoregressive passes per LLM step, yet no inference latency, RTF, or throughput measurements are reported; only training GPU hours are shown.

Several technical details are ambiguous or contradictory, including whether SRH runs in parallel or autoregressively, how ungrouped generated speech tokens are fed back into the LLM, how text and grouped speech sequences are exactly aligned, and how the 5Hz LLM output relates to the final 25Hz speech output.

Ablations are partial and mostly limited to Llama Questions and small-scale/small-model settings without CSE, so the full model's design choices are not comprehensively validated across benchmarks or metrics.

The manuscript contains citation errors (e.g., Freeze-Omni attributed to Défossez et al., MiniCPM-o 2.6 to Yao et al., Kimi-Audio to Xu et al.), which reduce confidence in the related-work and baseline positioning.
Ethical concerns are not addressed despite speech generation and voice conversation capabilities, including potential misuse for voice cloning, deepfakes, consent, watermarking, and dual-use risks.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the submission: code and checkpoints are promised but not provided, and training details for the speech tokenizer, speech encoder, adapter, and detokenizer are insufficient.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: joint speech-text autoregressive modeling for voice conversation, and the proposed dual-resolution idea of reducing the LLM input rate to 5Hz is intuitive and worth exploring.

The architecture combines several reasonable components—speech token grouping, a Speech Refined Head (SRH), and CoM-Mixing training—and the paper reports ablations suggesting each component contributes to performance.

The reported results on Llama Questions and Web Questions are strong in some settings, especially for the smaller model, and the paper promises code and checkpoint release, which could aid reproducibility if delivered.
weaknesses: Evaluation is too narrow for the SOTA claims: only two spoken QA benchmarks are used, with no broader dialogue, full-duplex, ASR, TTS naturalness, or human evaluation. This is insufficient to establish a new state of the art in voice conversation.

Baseline comparisons are not well controlled. Many baseline numbers are copied from other papers with different training data, prompts, decoding setups, model sizes, and tokenizer choices. The 8B improvements over prior SOTA are marginal (e.g., S2T 75.1 vs 74.7, S2S 55.5 vs 54.9) and may not be statistically meaningful.

The claimed SOTA with 'relatively small amount of data' is not supported: the paper does not provide controlled data-scaling comparisons against baselines, nor does it report the baselines' training data budgets or compute.

Novelty is limited. Parallel speech-text generation already exists (e.g., Moshi), and the proposed grouping, SRH, and CoM-Mixing read as incremental combinations of existing ideas. CoM-Mixing is essentially data augmentation/curriculum learning rather than a fundamentally new method.

The ablation study is poorly described and potentially confounded. It is unclear whether rows such as 'w/o SRH-Pretraining' also remove other components, why 'w/o CSE' outperforms 'w/o SRH-Pretraining' on several speech tasks, and how the SRH is initialized by pretraining a separate small LLM.

Reproducibility details are insufficient. The SRH pretraining data is described only as 'speech-text Alignment data', the loss weights λ and μ are not specified, architecture dimensions are missing, and the synthesis/training data construction is not detailed enough to reproduce.

The frame-rate reporting is potentially misleading: the table lists 5/5 for DrVoice, but SRH still performs k autoregressive forward passes to produce 25Hz speech tokens. The true output-side computational cost and latency are not transparently accounted for.

Speech quality is weaker than some baselines: UTMOS is lower than GLM-4-Voice, and the paper acknowledges this but does not address it. For a voice conversation system, naturalness and intelligibility are central, not secondary.
There is no discussion of safety, ethics, or misuse risks, such as voice cloning, impersonation, or synthetic speech generation without consent. This is a notable omission for a top-tier AI venue.
Writing and notation need substantial cleanup. Equation (3) appears malformed, Equation (2) is redundant/incorrectly written, and the architectural description around SRH and ungrouping is ambiguous.

strengths: Proposes dual-resolution speech representations that group 25Hz speech tokens to 5Hz for LLM input, reducing sequence length and better matching text token rates, with a Speech Refined Head (SRH) to recover fine-grained speech tokens during generation.

Introduces a CoM-Mixing training strategy over seven interaction patterns, enabling flexible text-only, speech+text, and chain-of-modality output modes; ablation shows clear benefit for speech generation.
Reports strong empirical results on Llama Questions and Web Questions, especially for speech-to-speech generation and for the smaller DrVoice-Small model.
Ablation studies analyze grouping factor, Continuous Speech Encoder, SRH, SRH pretraining, and CoM-Mixing, providing some evidence for the architectural choices.
Demonstrates substantial compute savings from grouping (e.g., ~50% GPU-hour reduction when grouping factor increases from 1 to 5), which is a practical efficiency advantage.
Writing and architecture diagram make the overall system relatively understandable, and the authors promise code/checkpoint release for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is very narrow: only two Spoken QA benchmarks are used, with no dialogue-level, instruction-following, full-duplex, or interactive speech evaluation, despite the paper framing the work as a voice conversation model.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: S2T results are copied from prior papers, S2S results from another prior paper, and baselines are not re-evaluated under the same prompts, decoding, tokenizer, or ASR setup.

The claimed SOTA is not supported "across the board": DrVoice is worse than Kimi-Audio on Web Questions S2T (65.2 vs 70.0) and worse than VITA-Audio on Web Questions S2S (40.1 vs 41.7). Main average gains over SOTA are also small and lack variance/statistical significance testing.

Novelty is incremental: the grouping/ungrouping and SRH design is closely related to prior multi-token prediction/parallel speech-text work, and CoM-Mixing mainly augments existing Chain-of-Modality data rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

There is a technical inconsistency around SRH latency: the paper says each LLM inference triggers k SRH executions and that SRH autoregressively generates k speech tokens, yet it claims low-latency/parallel speech-text generation. No inference latency or throughput measurements are reported.
Equation 3 is malformed in the manuscript (missing the speech-token argument in the concatenation), and key training hyperparameters such as lambda and mu in the multi-task loss are not specified.

Speech quality is not competitive with several baselines: UTMOS is lower than GLM-4-Voice, Moshi, and Llama-Omni, even though ASR-WER is better; the authors acknowledge limited naturalness but the claim of high-quality voice conversation remains weakly supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no dataset release details, filtering procedures, or full training configurations are provided; the promise to release code/checkpoints is useful but not yet verifiable from the manuscript.

Citation and table issues reduce confidence: e.g., Freeze-Omni is attributed to Défossez et al. (2024), Kimi-Audio is cited as Xu et al. (2025) in places, and some reported averages appear inconsistent or formatting-garbled.
Ablations are primarily on Llama Questions, often with small data subsets and no results on Web Questions; this weakens the generality of the conclusions about grouping, SRH, and CoM-Mixing.
Ethical and safety considerations for voice generation/misuse are not discussed, which is increasingly expected for speech generation models.

strengths: Proposes DrVoice, a parallel speech-text voice conversation model with dual-resolution speech representations that reduces the LLM frame rate to 5Hz while using a Speech Refined Head (SRH) to generate ungrouped speech tokens, which is a well-motivated direction for addressing speech-text frequency mismatch and computational cost.

Reports strong empirical results among ~7B models: new SOTA on OpenAudioBench overall (69.24) and Big Bench Audio (66.3), with competitive VoiceBench performance (76.02) and reasonable speech quality (UTMOS 4.29).
Includes extensive ablations on continuous speech encoder, SRH, SRH pretraining, grouping factor, CoM-Mixing, and training strategy, providing useful insight into component contributions.

Introduces practical training and inference controls, including CoM-Mixing with seven interaction patterns and Core-Cocktail training, enabling flexible text-only, parallel speech-text, and chain-of-modality generation.

Shows engineering effort with large-scale data (~100K hours pretraining, ~26K hours speech-to-speech conversation) and demonstrates that a low LLM frame rate can still yield competitive benchmark performance.
weaknesses: The Core-Cocktail training description is internally inconsistent: the appendix sets the interpolation weight alpha = 0, which makes M_r = M_0 and completely discards the Stage-1 model. This undermines the claimed benefit of merging Stage-1 and base LLM parameters and makes the Stage-2 improvement difficult to attribute to the proposed strategy.

Important technical details and equations are unclear or erroneous: Eq. 3 appears to concatenate discrete speech tokens before a linear layer, the dimension d_test is likely a typo, and the interaction between user-end continuous Whisper features, assistant-end S3Tokenizer tokens, grouping, ungroupping, and padding with <SIL> is not precisely specified.

The efficiency claim is not fully validated. Although the LLM backbone operates at 5Hz, SRH performs k autoregressive forward passes to generate k speech tokens per grouped step and is initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B; inference latency, throughput, and real-time factor are not reported, so the practical cost reduction over 12.5/25Hz baselines remains unclear.

Evaluation has notable gaps. UltraEval-Audio performance (47.66) is below Qwen2.5-Omni (50.46), Baichuan-Omni-1.5 (48.67), and MiniCPM-o 2.6 (48.05), so the claim of being comparable to SOTA there is overstated. ASR-WER (11.2) is substantially worse than Qwen2.5-Omni (3.48), and no human evaluation is provided for naturalness, prosody, emotion, or conversational quality.

Novelty is incremental: low-frame-rate speech token grouping and separate speech decoders/heads are related to prior work, while CoM-Mixing and Core-Cocktail are adaptations of existing chain-of-modality and model-merging ideas. The contribution is mainly a combination and engineering effort rather than a fundamentally new method.

Ablation results are partially inconsistent and limited: Table 4 reports the same S2T score (56.00) for w/o SRH-Pretraining and w/o SRH, while the text describes different relative drops. Most ablations use DrVoice-Small (1.5B) and reduced data, so conclusions may not fully transfer to the final 7B model.

Reproducibility is limited: training data include large synthesized and in-house corpora, details of data filtering and prompt construction are incomplete, no code or model release is indicated, and the training requires substantial compute, making independent replication difficult.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully controlled, as models were trained on different data and compute budgets; some baseline numbers are cited from other papers, which raises possible protocol mismatch concerns.

The reported SOTA margin on OpenAudioBench over Kimi-Audio is very small (69.24 vs. 69.08 overall), and the paper does not provide statistical significance or detailed per-task analysis to establish that the improvement is robust.

strengths: Targets an important problem: efficient end-to-end spoken dialogue with parallel speech-text generation.
The dual-resolution idea is intuitive: group speech tokens to reduce the LLM input frame rate to 5Hz while using an ungrouping/refinement head to recover fine-grained speech tokens.
The paper reports experiments on several relevant benchmarks and includes ablations on grouping, SRH, CSE, and training strategies.
Big Bench Audio results are notably strong compared with the listed baselines.
The grouping strategy is shown to reduce GPU hours in ablation, supporting the efficiency motivation.
The system-prompt-based interaction patterns provide flexibility across text-only, speech-only, and joint generation settings.
weaknesses: Fatal technical issue in the Core-Cocktail training strategy: the implementation details state the interpolation weight is set to alpha = 0. With M_r = alpha M1 + (1 - alpha) M0, alpha = 0 means M_r = M0, so Stage 1 training is completely discarded and Stage 2 simply fine-tunes the base LLM. The claimed recovery from 70.19 to 74.73 cannot then be attributed to the proposed strategy, which invalidates a central training contribution.

The SOTA claims are substantially overstated. OpenAudioBench improvement over Kimi-Audio is only +0.16 overall (69.24 vs 69.08), VoiceBench is below Kimi-Audio (76.02 vs 76.93), and UltraEval-Audio is below Qwen2.5-Omni, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, and MiniCPM-o. The paper nonetheless describes the model as a new SOTA and leading open-source speech foundation model.

The computational-efficiency claim is not properly supported. Although the LLM backbone sees 5Hz grouped speech representations, the Speech Refined Head generates individual speech tokens via k autoregressive forward passes, so the effective speech-token output rate and generation cost are closer to 25Hz than 5Hz. End-to-end latency, FLOPs, and memory costs are not reported.

Speech-generation quality is weaker than claimed: ASR-WER is 11.2 versus Qwen2.5-Omni's 3.48 and Step-Audio2-Mini's 9.5, and UTMOS is 4.29 versus Step-Audio2-Mini's 4.53. The paper acknowledges the gap but still frames the results as high-quality and well-aligned.

Architecture and loss details are unclear. The alignment/padding mechanism using <SIL> for mismatched speech-text lengths, the text-head loss over length T, inference termination, and the exact conditioning of SRH on H_{<i} are not well specified. Eq. 3 is also ambiguous about whether s_j are token IDs or embeddings.

There is an inconsistency about SRH initialization: Section 3.3 says it is initialized from a pre-trained TTS model, while Appendix A says Qwen2.5-0.5B is trained with a T2M paradigm to initialize SRH. This makes reproducibility and the ablation interpretation difficult.

Novelty is incremental. Grouping speech tokens is closely related to prior parallel multi-token prediction work, SRH is essentially a TTS-style refinement head, CoM-Mixing draws on chain-of-modality prompting, and Core-Cocktail is adapted from LM-Cocktail. The paper does not clearly isolate what is fundamentally new beyond the combination.

Important evaluation details are missing. Big Bench Audio is used as a headline benchmark but is not described or cited. No human evaluation is provided for naturalness, speaker similarity, emotion, or prosody. There are no significance tests for marginal wins such as OpenAudioBench.

Ablations are mostly conducted on DrVoice-Small (1.5B), so the key architectural and training claims for the 7B model are not directly validated. Some ablation comparisons are confounded, e.g., comparing 'w/o CSE' to 'w/o SRH-Pretraining' to infer the effect of SRH pretraining.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair because DRVOICE is evaluated with carefully designed system prompts while baselines may use default inference setups. The paper also omits relevant parallel speech-text baselines such as Moshi despite discussing it in related work.

The manuscript has many clarity and presentation issues: inconsistent capitalization (DRVOICE/DrVoice), typos such as 'machinism', 'Delsz', 'Borsoś', unclear figure labels, and inconsistent notation. These make the technical presentation harder to trust and reproduce.
Ethical considerations for voice cloning, synthetic speech misuse, and impersonation are not discussed, despite the model being a speech generation system trained partly on synthesized speech.

strengths: Proposes a novel dual-resolution speech representation: grouping 25Hz speech tokens to 5Hz for LLM input, reducing computational cost and better matching text token rates, while using a Speech Refined Head to ungroup and autoregressively generate individual speech tokens.

Achieves strong empirical results: DRVOICE-7B reports new SOTA on OpenAudioBench and Big Bench Audio, with competitive performance on VoiceBench and UltraEval-Audio in the ~7B open-source speech foundation model class.

Significant efficiency benefit: operating the LLM backbone at 5Hz input/output dramatically lowers sequence length and GPU hours, with grouping factor 5 reducing nearly 50% GPU hours in the reported ablation.

Includes a substantial ablation suite covering continuous speech encoder, SRH, SRH pretraining, grouping factor, CoM-Mixing, data scaling, data quality, and Core-Cocktail training, which helps isolate component contributions.

The paper is clearly written and well positioned relative to text-driven, interleaved, and parallel speech-text models, with a helpful taxonomy and system-prompt design for multiple interaction modes.
Despite the low 5Hz frame rate, speech quality remains reasonably competitive (UTMOS 4.29), showing the proposed compression/ungrouping mechanism can preserve intelligibility and overall quality.
weaknesses: The Core-Cocktail training strategy is internally inconsistent: the appendix sets the interpolation weight alpha = 0, which makes M_r equal to the base LLM M_0 and discards all Stage-1 parameters. This contradicts the claimed merging benefit and calls into question the necessity and validity of the two-stage training ablation.

The parallel autoregressive feedback mechanism is not fully specified: it is unclear how the individual speech tokens generated by SRH are fed back into the 5Hz LLM, whether the LLM receives grouped speech embeddings, individual speech tokens, or hidden states, and how this aligns with the equations for c_t and s_t.

SOTA claims are somewhat overstated. OpenAudioBench improvement over Kimi-Audio is marginal (69.24 vs 69.08), and DRVOICE is not SOTA on VoiceBench (76.02 vs 76.93) or UltraEval-Audio (47.66 vs 50.46). The paper more accurately achieves SOTA only on OpenAudioBench and Big Bench Audio.

Speech-text alignment is notably weaker than leading systems: ASR-WER is 11.2, much worse than Qwen2.5-Omni (3.48) and Step-Audio2-Mini (9.5). This undercuts the claim that the method fully addresses speech generation quality, even though it is acknowledged in limitations.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are reported, and some baseline numbers are generated by the authors without full decoding/hyperparameter details. The Big Bench Audio improvement is large but would benefit from deeper verification and analysis.

Ablations are mostly performed on DRVOICE-Small (1.5B) with subset data, so it is unclear whether conclusions transfer to the 7B model. Core-Cocktail analysis is also presented mainly on VoiceBench T2T text metrics rather than the main speech-to-speech setting.

Reproducibility is limited: training relies heavily on in-house/synthesized data, large-scale pretraining, and frozen components from CosyVoice, with no clear indication that code, checkpoints, or data recipes will be released. This makes it difficult to verify the claimed SOTA results independently.

There are notation and presentation issues, including malformed equations, unclear symbol definitions (e.g., d_test, H_<i, splitting/ungrouping), and inconsistent terminology between CSE and continuous audio encoder; these hinder full understanding of the technical design.
